docs.title: Block Diagram
docs.text:
Motor Control Subsystem

Overview

This block diagram illustrates the Motor Control and Power Distribution subsystem used in the EGR 304 robotic platform. The subsystem is responsible for regulated power distribution, motor control, feedback monitoring, and communication between the control electronics and mechanical drive components.

The design utilizes a 12 VDC power source protected by a fuse and regulated to provide stable operating voltages for the control circuitry. A Curiosity Nano microcontroller generates the control signals required by the left and right motor driver circuits. These motor drivers provide the necessary current and voltage to operate the differential drive motors.

Encoder feedback from both motors is routed back to the microcontroller, allowing motor speed and position monitoring. Debug LEDs are included to provide visual indicators during testing, troubleshooting, and normal operation.

Power Source

• 12 V DC Barrel Jack Input • Fuse Protection Circuit • Voltage Regulation Circuit • Decoupling Capacitor Network • Common Ground Reference

Controller

• Curiosity Nano Microcontroller

Actuators

• Left Drive Motor • Right Drive Motor

Sensors • Motor Encoder Feedback Signals • User Input Switch

Indicators

• Status LED • Debug LEDs

Team Interfaces

• Connector interface for signal routing and communication between subsystem components and team-designed modules

Block Diagram

Functional Description

Power enters the subsystem through a 12 VDC barrel jack and passes through a protective fuse before being distributed throughout the system. A voltage regulator conditions the incoming voltage and provides the required operating voltage for the control electronics.

The Curiosity Nano microcontroller processes control logic and outputs motor control signals to the left and right motor driver circuits. Each motor driver independently controls a DC motor, enabling differential drive operation and directional control.

Encoder feedback from each motor is returned to the microcontroller where it can be used to monitor motor performance and support future closed-loop control implementations. Status LEDs and debugging indicators provide visual confirmation of subsystem activity and assist in system validation.

This subsystem serves as the central interface between the power distribution network, control electronics, sensor feedback circuits, and mechanical drive components of the robotic platform.

docs.title: Motor Driver Subsystem – H‑Bridge
docs.text: Option Pros Cons Photo Link Cost L298N Dual H‑Bridge (Arduino Albers) Inexpensive dual‑channel driver; can control two DC motors (Left + Right) with forward/reverse. Widely used and documented. Tons of tutorials, wiring diagrams, and example code online. Built‑in flyback diodes protect the driver from motor inductive spikes. Simple to interface with PIC, Arduino, Raspberry Pi. On‑board 5V regulator. Large voltage drop (~2V) → motors receive less voltage, reducing torque and speed. Low efficiency (bipolar transistors) → runs hot and wastes power. Limited current capability (0.8–1.2A continuous). Old design replaced by MOSFET drivers (TB6612FNG, DRV8833, BTS7960). Bulky module. Weak 5V regulator → often must be disabled. (add image) product link $15.39 DRV8833 – KOOBOOK 1.5A Dual H‑Bridge Modern MOSFET design → far more efficient than L298N (almost no voltage drop). Low heat generation → runs cool under load. Wide voltage range (2.7V–10.8V). Dual motor support (forward/reverse). High efficiency → better motor torque. Low standby current → ideal for low‑power embedded systems. Lower maximum current (1.5A peak, ~1A continuous). Not ideal for large or high‑torque motors. Not suitable for 12V motors. Small module size → easier to damage. Requires careful wiring (small pins). No built‑in 5V regulator. (add image) product link $8.99 A3909GLYTR‑T (Allegro) Modern MOSFET design → highly efficient, minimal voltage drop. Dual H‑bridge → can independently drive two DC motors or one stepper. Wide voltage range (2.4V–5.5V). Low power consumption → excellent for battery‑powered devices. High PWM frequency → smooth motor control, low audible noise. Very small QFN package → extremely difficult to solder by hand. Low voltage limit (max ~5.5V). Lower current capability (500–700mA per channel). Requires external components (decoupling caps, layout). Bare IC → no screw terminals or breakout board. (add image) product link $1.82

docs.title: Right/Left DC Motor
docs.text: Option Pros Cons Photo Link Cost 24V – 1800 RPM Slow‑Speed DC Motor Very inexpensive → great for budget builds or prototypes. Lightweight and compact → easy to mount. High RPM → good for lightweight applications. Easy to power (3–12V). Widely available. Low torque → struggles with heavier loads. No datasheet → specs vary widely. Inconsistent quality (eBay). No encoder → cannot measure speed/position. Short lifespan → brushes wear quickly. RPM fluctuates with voltage. (add image) product link $19.95 JOHNSON ELECTRIC – C4557‑60003 – HC615LG – 65701 (6–18VDC) Higher torque → better for wheels, lifting loads, pushing weight. Metal housing → more durable. Better suited for real robotics → handles friction and load. More stable RPM under load. Higher current draw → may exceed limits of DRV8833/TB6612FNG. No datasheet → exact torque, RPM, stall current unknown. Bulkier and heavier → requires stronger mounting. Quality varies (eBay). No encoder. May require heatsinking. (add image) product link $8.98 BOJACK Type 130 EK1450 Mini DC Motors (3–6V) Comes in a multi‑pack → good for testing or replacing motors. Standardized size (130) → easy to find mounts. Decent RPM → good for small robots or fans. Runs on 3–6V → compatible with DRV8833. Better consistency than random eBay motors. Low torque → not suitable for heavy loads. Still lacks detailed datasheets. No encoder → cannot measure rotation or speed. Not designed for 9–12V systems → may overheat or burn out. Not ideal for long‑term robotics → hobby‑grade. (add image) product link $8.98

docs.title: Voltage Regulator (5V Rail)
docs.text: Option Pros Cons Photo Link Price Microchip LDO (SOT‑23‑5) Ultra‑low dropout → maintains stable 5V output even when input voltage is only slightly higher. Very low quiescent current → excellent for battery‑powered systems. High output accuracy → tight regulation for sensitive logic circuits. Built‑in protection (thermal shutdown + current limiting). Small footprint → ideal for compact PCBs. Low noise output → good for analog circuits and microcontroller logic. Low current capability (300–500mA) → not enough for motors. Requires careful PCB layout. Linear regulator → inefficient when dropping from high input voltages (9V→5V). Generates heat under load. Not ideal for electromechanical systems → best for logic only. (add image) product link $2.41 Automotive‑Grade 5V Regulator Automotive‑grade reliability → designed for harsh environments, vibration, temperature extremes. Very stable 5V output → excellent regulation. Low dropout voltage. High input voltage tolerance (up to 40V). Built‑in protections (overcurrent, thermal shutdown, reverse‑battery). Good for embedded systems → robust and predictable. Lower current capability (150–300mA). Linear regulator → inefficient for high voltage drops (12V→5V). Requires heatsinking under moderate load. More expensive than basic LDOs. Not ideal for powering electromechanical components → best for logic. (add image) product link $8.99
